solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Company satisfied with one’s rubbish mobile being returned, as special purchase (10,4)

indicators.note: something returned comes back the way it went, so the letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: CO is the usual abbreviation for company
to meet a need is to satisfy it
one's = one is, so I + S
rot = nonsense, rubbish
a cell (phone) is a mobile

annotation.surface: A firm pleased to be sent back a scrapped phone, treating it as a prized acquisition.
annotation.walkthrough: Only the four pieces after 'Company' are turned round; CO stays where it is at the front. 'Mobile' is a noun here, the phone, not an anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A collector's item is something bought because it is rare or special.

entries.clue: German agreed to get French right on board (5)

indicators.note: placed right on something is set immediately beside it, so JA comes straight after OUI

blocks.note: the French word for yes
German for yes, placed right on (immediately after) the French

annotation.surface: A German agrees to bring a French speaker properly into the team.
annotation.walkthrough: The Ouija board's name is itself French yes plus German yes, so the wordplay retells the word's origin. 'On board' looks like a phrase meaning 'in agreement', but 'board' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A Ouija board is the lettered board used at seances.

entries.clue: Looked unpleasantly twisted when swapping sides (6)

indicators.note: the two sides are left and right, L and R, and swapping them trades those letters' places

blocks.note: reeled = staggered, spun round; this is the word worked on
left and right, L and R: each takes the other's position in the word

annotation.surface: Someone pulled a nasty face when two parties changed allegiance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sides' means left and right, L and R, so swapping them exchanges those two letters inside REELED.
annotation.definitionFit: To leer is to look at someone in a sly or lascivious way.

entries.clue: Bulletin needs bit of punctuation – not a one-off (10)

indicators.note: 'not a' simply removes the letter A from the word before it

blocks.note: COMMA without its A
unique = one of a kind

annotation.surface: A news notice that wants a comma added, not as a one-time fix.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'not a one-off' read as a phrase; split it so 'not a' works on COMMA and 'one-off' stands alone.
annotation.definitionFit: An official statement issued to the press is a bulletin in the plain sense, and the word comes straight from French for 'communicated'.

entries.clue: Has sprint legend cut energy? (4)

indicators.note: what is cut is taken out, so E goes

blocks.note: Jesse Owens, four-time Olympic gold medallist in 1936
E (energy) removed from OWENS

annotation.surface: Did a great sprinter run out of steam?
annotation.walkthrough: 'Has' opens the clue looking like the start of a question, but it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: possession, as in 'she has a car', is ownership.

entries.clue: Turn a pair of taps, this produces water when you’re boiling (7)

definitions.text: this produces water when you’re boiling

blocks.note: spin = turn
as written
taps are labelled C (cold) and H (hot)

annotation.surface: Instructions for running water from two taps when you're overheated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'You're boiling' sounds like feeling hot, but it means you are boiling the vegetable, which leaks a surprising amount of water into the pan.
annotation.definitionFit: Spinach wilts and releases lots of water when boiled.

entries.clue: Worker who gives rise to loot? (9)

blocks.note: loot = stolen goods, the word that is turned up
one who gives rise to something creates it, a maker

annotation.surface: A labourer who somehow generates stolen goods.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rise' works twice: someone who gives rise to a thing makes it, and making LOOT rise in a down entry flips it to TOOL. The question mark owns up to that double duty.
annotation.definitionFit: A craftsman who makes jigs, dies and cutting tools for industry is, plainly, a skilled worker.

indicators.note: in a down clue, what rises reads from the bottom up, so LOOT turns into TOOL

entries.clue: Nick will be married in Paris if up and fit (14)

indicators.note: what is said in Paris is said in French, so 'if' becomes SI
in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, turning SI into IS

blocks.note: m. = married, as in genealogy tables
French for 'if' is SI, written upwards in this down clue
appropriate = fitting, suitable

annotation.surface: Nick will marry in Paris provided he is out of bed and healthy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a man's name but is the verb: in British slang to nick is to steal.
annotation.definitionFit: To misappropriate is to take dishonestly, which is what nicking is.

entries.clue: Rocky bridge from Sting EP on piano’s dividing old group (8,6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing on another sits above it, so EP comes before P
what divides something splits it in two, so EPP goes into STING

blocks.note: as written
as written: an extended-play record
p = piano, quiet, in music; EP sits on it, giving EPP
EPP splits STING into ST...ING, making STEPPING
the (Rolling) Stones, a band of long standing

annotation.surface: An old band's gig interrupted by a Sting record played on piano.
annotation.walkthrough: The music surface (Sting, EP, piano, group) hides a row of rocks across a stream. Sting is not solved for its meaning; its letters are simply split.
annotation.definitionFit: Stepping stones are a line of stones set across water to cross it.

entries.clue: Chap in race animated barmiest finish in marathon (9)

indicators.note: animated means lively and in motion, so the letters are set moving
the finish of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: anagram fodder
last letter of marathoN

annotation.surface: A man in a running race finishes the marathon in the wildest state of excitement.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Race' reads as a running race, but it means a people or tribe. Barmy is British slang for crazy.
annotation.definitionFit: A tribesman is a man belonging to a tribe, a race of people.

entries.clue: I party less, having no need for insiders and stars (5)

indicators.note: doing without the insiders removes the inner letters, leaving only the outer ones

blocks.note: as written
a do is a party

blocks.clueFragment: less, having no need for insiders
blocks.note: LESS with its inside letters ES dropped

annotation.surface: A would-be celebrity claims to go out less, needing no inside friends.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Insiders' means the inner letters of the word just before it, not people.
annotation.definitionFit: Idols are stars, celebrities worshipped by fans.

entries.clue: Level, leapt extraordinarily, followed by gold (7)

indicators.note: what happens extraordinarily departs from the ordinary order, so the letters are rearranged
what follows comes after, so AU goes at the end

blocks.note: anagram of LEAPT
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

annotation.surface: A jumper cleared the bar in extraordinary style and took the gold.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Level' opens the clue looking like an adjective, but it is the noun: a plateau is a level stretch, or a stage where progress levels off.
annotation.definitionFit: A plateau is a level area of high ground.

entries.clue: Combat uniform required in Military Police’s preparation for conflict? (4-2)

indicators.note: what is required in something has to go inside it

blocks.note: war = combat
the initials M and P of Military Police
U is Uniform in the NATO alphabet, placed inside MP

annotation.surface: Battle fatigues are compulsory for military police getting ready for a fight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Combat uniform' is one phrase in the surface but splits in two. The question mark covers the stretch: a warm-up readies athletes for a contest, not literally a war.
annotation.definitionFit: A warm-up is preparation before a contest, playfully called conflict here.

entries.clue: Incite riots about Jamaican music genre, primarily for sport (3-7)

indicators.note: to riot is to run wild, so the letters of INCITE are thrown into disorder
one thing about another goes round it
primarily means first, so take the first letter

blocks.note: anagram of INCITE, split around SKA
ska is a Jamaican music style, forerunner of reggae
first letter of Genre

annotation.surface: A Jamaican music scene stirs up trouble, mainly for fun.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Riots' looks like the object of 'Incite', but it is a verb telling INCITE's letters to run wild.
annotation.definitionFit: Gliding on blades over a rink is a competitive Olympic sport as well as a pastime, a definition by category.

entries.clue: More than one troublemaker is surrounding person who’s 16 (4)

indicators.note: what surrounds something goes round it, so IS encloses MP

blocks.note: as written
16 down is POLITICAL; an MP (Member of Parliament) is a political person, placed inside IS

annotation.surface: A roomful of troublemakers gathers round a politician.
annotation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points at 16 down, POLITICAL, so the person is a politician, MP.
annotation.definitionFit: Imps are mischievous troublemakers, usually children.

entries.clue: Vote to restrict CIA, it worked out of government (9)

indicators.note: to restrict something is to hem it in, so POLL goes round the rest
worked, as in worked dough, means kneaded into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: a poll is a vote
anagram of CIA IT, placed inside POLL

annotation.surface: A vote is held to rein in the CIA, and it works out.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma splits the surface so that 'it' seems to refer back to the vote; its two letters join the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: The adjective describing government and the state; the Greek polis, the city-state, underlies it.

entries.clue: Poor soul requesting pick-me-up, by the way? (5-5)

definitions.text: Poor soul requesting pick-me-up, by the way?

blocks.note: read as someone low asking for a tonic; meant as someone asking to be picked up, given a lift
read as a throwaway aside; meant literally, standing by the road

annotation.surface: A sorry figure casually asking for a drink or tonic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pick-me-up' reads as a tonic and 'by the way' as an aside; taken literally, the traveller asks to be picked up and waits beside the road.
annotation.definitionFit: A hitch-hiker stands by the road asking passing drivers for a lift.

entries.clue: Greens targeting drivers here? On the contrary (4,6)

definitions.text: Greens targeting drivers here? On the contrary

blocks.note: read as environmentalists going after motorists; greens and drivers are both golf words
swap the roles: drivers, the long-hitting clubs, target the greens

annotation.surface: Environmental campaigners going after motorists.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Greens' suggests environmentalists and 'drivers' motorists; 'on the contrary' swaps the roles, and both words turn out to be golf terms.
annotation.definitionFit: A golf course is where drivers (clubs) send balls towards greens.

entries.clue: Hoax Democrat used before November’s doom? (7)

blocks.note: a con is a hoax or swindle
Dem. is the abbreviation for Democrat
N is November in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: A fake Democrat spells disaster for the November elections.
annotation.walkthrough: 'November' suggests the US election month, but it only supplies the letter N.
annotation.definitionFit: Doom as a verb, to consign someone to an unhappy fate, is exactly what a court does when it condemns a prisoner.

entries.clue: Stumble in tango, leading to endless tears (4)

indicators.note: what leads to something comes before it, so T comes first
without an end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: T is Tango in the NATO alphabet
RIPS (tears) without its last letter

annotation.surface: A dancer falls over mid-tango and it ends in tears.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tears' are rips here, not crying; the surface's weeping is a decoy.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: catching your foot and losing balance, as in a trip on the stairs.

entries.clue: Tipsy choirmaster’s embraces one disturbed (6)

indicators.note: what embraces something holds it inside, so the answer sits within the words

blocks.note: tiPSY CHOirmaster: the letters sit across the two words

annotation.surface: A drunken choirmaster hugs a troubled chorister.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Embraces' reads as a hug, but it tells you the answer is held within the words before it.
annotation.definitionFit: A psycho is, informally, a mentally disturbed person.

entries.clue: They’re mighty birds with a new stuffing (6)

indicators.note: with here means joined by, so AN comes along
stuffing goes inside a bird, so AN is put inside TITS

blocks.note: tits are small songbirds
A plus N (new), stuffed inside TITS

annotation.surface: Some impressive birds come with a novel stuffing, as if for a roast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stuffing' fits the birds-for-dinner picture, but it tells you AN goes inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Titans are giants, people or things of great might.

entries.clue: Spike in marriages sadly going west (7)

indicators.note: the answer is held in the words that follow
on a map west is to the left, so the letters run right to left

blocks.note: marrIAGES SAdly, read from right to left

annotation.surface: A rise in the number of weddings that end badly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spike' reads as a surge in numbers, but it is a pointed weapon. 'Going west' also hints at things going wrong, which suits the sad marriages.
annotation.definitionFit: An assegai is a slender iron-tipped spear used in southern Africa.

entries.clue: Killjoy needs good seat (5)

blocks.note: g = good
rump = backside, seat

annotation.surface: A spoilsport wants a comfortable chair.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Seat' means the backside, not furniture.
annotation.definitionFit: A grump, a sulky and bad-tempered person, is the kind of killjoy who spoils others' fun.

entries.clue: Free trade, third reduced by 90 per cent (4)

indicators.note: cutting a number by ninety per cent leaves a tenth of it, so L (50) becomes V (5)

blocks.note: a sale is a piece of trade; this is the word worked on
the third letter L is Roman 50, and a tenth of it is 5, V, which takes its place

annotation.surface: A trade deal slashes a third of costs by nine-tenths.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Third' means the third letter of the word, and it must be read as a Roman numeral: L (50) shrinks to V (5).
annotation.definitionFit: Free as a verb, to release from danger, as a lifeguard saves a swimmer.

entries.clue: Hotel occupies particular special area (5)

indicators.note: what occupies a place sits inside it, so H goes into NICE

blocks.note: nice = particular, fussy, as in a nice distinction
H is Hotel in the NATO alphabet, placed inside NICE

annotation.surface: A hotel takes over an exclusive section of a building.
annotation.walkthrough: The old sense of nice as precise or fastidious is what matches 'particular'.
annotation.definitionFit: A special area of interest or trade, as in a niche market, borrows the word for a recess in a wall.

entries.clue: Disheartened over meeting date where fight took place (9)

indicators.note: losing heart means losing the middle, so AGAIN drops its central A
meeting means joining, so the two pieces are put together

blocks.note: AGAIN (over, once more) with its middle letter A removed
to court someone is to date them

annotation.surface: Someone crushed after a date recalls where a quarrel broke out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Over' means again, as in 'do it over'. Agincourt is the 1415 battle in northern France won by Henry V.
annotation.definitionFit: The Battle of Agincourt was fought there in 1415.

entries.clue: Something that gets under my skin? Huddles – they disrupt a party (8,6)

blocks.clueFragment: Something that gets under my skin?
blocks.note: a splinter literally lodges under the skin
huddles are tight groups

annotation.surface: An irritating guest crowds people into cliques and spoils the celebration.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gets under my skin' sounds like annoyance, but it is literal. 'Party' is a political party, not a celebration.
annotation.definitionFit: Splinter groups break away from a political party and divide it.
